_comment: Department of Basic Education Grade 10 Physical Sciences P2 (Chemistry), November 2018 national common examination.
Questions and marking-guideline answers extracted from the text layer of the official PDFs
(paper2.pdf, paper2_memo.pdf) and read against the rendered pages. The guideline is
bilingual (English/Afrikaans); only the English is transcribed. memo_answer gives the guideline's
working and final answers (tick marks removed); diagrams, graphs and circuits are described in
brackets in the question text. Data sheets printed with the paper are not transcribed.
FORMAT: 150 marks, 2 hours, ten compulsory questions (Q1 multiple choice 20 marks). The marking
guideline instructs markers to ignore QUESTION 1.4 (no correct option) and QUESTION 8.4 (molecular
formula is not in CAPS for Grade 10) and to mark out of 141; both questions are kept here with a
memo_note, and total_marks stays at the printed 150.

questions.context: QUESTION 1: MULTIPLE-CHOICE QUESTIONS. Various options are provided as possible answers to the following questions. Each question has only ONE correct answer. questions.text: What is the trend in ionisation energy as you move from element P to element R? Write down only INCREASES, DECREASES or REMAINS THE SAME. Explain the answer.
questions.memo_answer:
Increases.
From P to R the atomic radius gets smaller / the outer electrons get closer to the nucleus.
The attraction between the nucleus and the outer electrons gets stronger, so more energy is needed to remove the electrons.

questions.context: QUESTION 5 (Start on a new page.) Study the physical and chemical processes below and answer the questions that follow. X: H2O(s) → H2O(g); Y: CaCO3(s) → (heat, ∆) CaO(s) + CO2(g); Z: iron + oxygen → iron(III) oxide

A change in which no new substances are formed.
OR A change in which energy changes are small in relation to chemical changes.

questions.context: 5.6 A 20 g sample of CaCO3(s) in process Y decomposes to form 11,2 g of CaO. In a second sample, 30 g decomposes to form x g of CO2.
questions.text: State the law of constant composition.
questions.memo_answer: No matter how a chemical compound is prepared, it always contains the same elements in the same proportion by mass.

questions.text: Use the law in QUESTION 5.6.1 to calculate mass x of the CO2 formed.
questions.memo_answer:
OPTION 1: mass of CO2 in the 1st sample = 20 - 11,2 = 8,8 g; proportion of CO2 = 8,8/20; mass of CO2 in the 2nd sample = 8,8/20 x 30 = 13,2 g
OPTION 2: 100 g CaCO3 → 44 g CO2; 30 g CaCO3 → x g CO2; x = 30 x 44 / 100 = 13,2 g
OPTION 3: 20 g CaCO3 → 11,2 g CaO; 30 g CaCO3 → 16,83 g CaO; mass of CO2 = 30 - 16,83 = 13,2 g

questions.text: The substance tested in Experiment 3 was analysed. It was found to contain 40% carbon, 6,67% hydrogen and 53,33% oxygen. Determine the molecular formula if the molar mass is 180 g∙mol-1.
questions.topic: Quantitative aspects: concentration and empirical formula
questions.memo_answer:
Assume a 100 g sample: n(C) : n(H) : n(O) = 40/12 : 6,67/1 : 53,33/16 = 3,33 : 6,67 : 3,33 = 1 : 2 : 1
Empirical formula: CH2O
M(CH2O) = 12 + 2 + 16 = 30 g·mol⁻¹; factor = 180 / 30 = 6
Molecular formula: C6H12O6
questions.memo_note: The guideline instructs markers to ignore this question (molecular formula is not in the Grade 10 CAPS); the paper is marked out of 141.

questions.context: QUESTION 10 (Start on a new page.) The diagram below shows how the hydrosphere is linked to the biosphere. Study the diagram and answer the questions that follow. [Diagram: PLANTS → (A) → water vapour → (B) → CLOUDS → (C) → back to PLANTS.]
questions.text: Differentiate between the hydrosphere and biosphere.
questions.memo_answer:
Hydrosphere: includes all the water of the earth (found as liquid water, ice and water vapour).
Biosphere: includes all the living organisms.

questions.text: A
B
C
Describe the energy changes during processes A and B. Write down only ENERGY GAINED or ENERGY LOST.
Describe the interaction between the hydrosphere and plants.
questions.memo_answer:
Roots of plants absorb water from the ground.
Plants release the water to the atmosphere by transpiration.
The water condenses to form clouds.
Then water falls back to the ground by precipitation.
